> **Internal / deep-dive doc.** Companion to `dev/security_model.Rmd`. Concrete
> knobs and host steps to tighten a hal deployment. Lives in `dev/` (ships in
> the repo, not on the public site). Read the trust model first — these knobs
> are guardrails unless paired with OS/VM isolation.

# 1. Pick a permission posture

The biggest single lever. Default is open (`auto-allow`); tighten per session or
globally.

```r
# Prompt before every tool call (interactive sessions)
hal_configure(permission_policy = "ask")

# Deny everything (read-only chat; eval_r/tool calls refused)
hal_configure(permission_policy = "auto-deny")
```

A **function policy** gives fine-grained, programmable control. It receives
`list(backend, tool_name, input)` and returns a string containing `"allow"` or
`"deny"`:

```r
hal_configure(permission_policy = function(p) {
  # Allow inspection, deny anything that writes/destroys via eval_r.
  if (p$tool_name == "eval_r") {
    code <- p$input$code %||% ""
    if (grepl("unlink|file\\.remove|writeLines|system|download\\.file", code)) {
      return("deny: looks destructive")
    }
  }
  "allow"
})
```

Takes effect on next session init — call `hal_reset()` to apply immediately.
Note the function policy round-trips through MCP on the Claude backend only when
you supply a function (it drives `--permission-prompt-tool`).

# 2. Outbound secret handling

The scanner runs on text headed to the model (prompts, env snapshots, `eval_r`
output). Default is `warn` (detect + warn, still send). Tighten:

```r
hal_configure(credential_action = "redact")  # scrub detected secrets, then send
hal_configure(credential_action = "block")   # abort the call entirely
```

Detected shapes (see `R/governance.R`): GitHub tokens (`ghp_`/`gho_`/`ghs_`/
`ghr_`/fine-grained), OpenAI (`sk-`, `sk-proj-`, `sk-svcacct-`, `sk-admin-`),
Anthropic (`sk-ant-`), AWS access/secret keys, Google API keys (`AIza…`), Slack
tokens + webhooks, PEM private-key blocks, and quoted `key = "…"` assignments.
It also redacts the live values of known sensitive env vars
(`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`, …).

**This is best-effort.** A novel token shape or an arbitrary secret file will
pass through. Don't treat `redact` as a guarantee — pair it with not exposing
the secret to the session in the first place.

# 3. Constrain `eval_r`

The denylist is a guardrail (bypassable — see the trust model), but it still
catches the obvious first attempt. Customize or extend it:

```r
# Add to the default set
hal_configure(eval_denylist = c(hal:::.HAL_DEFAULT_EVAL_DENYLIST,
                                "readRDS", "load", "readLines"))

# Disable entirely (full access — only if you trust the whole loop)
hal_configure(eval_denylist = FALSE)
```

Bound runaway code:

```r
hal_configure(eval_timeout = 15)   # seconds per eval_r call
```

`eval_timeout` uses `setTimeLimit`, which interrupts at interpreter checkpoints —
a blocking C call or external I/O may not be cut off. For a hard wall, run hal
under an OS-level resource limit.

# 4. Multi-user / shared hosts

- The IPC directory (parent ↔ MCP subprocess) is created **`0700`**
  (`R/tool-eval-r.R`) inside R's per-session `tempdir()` (itself `0700` on
  POSIX). This keeps another local user from dropping a `request-*.json`
  (code injection into your session) or reading eval results. If you override
  `TMPDIR` to a shared, loosely-permissioned location, restore `0700` semantics
  there.
- On Windows, `%TEMP%` is per-user, so the IPC dir is already private; `mode`
  is ignored.
- The MCP subprocess runs with `--vanilla`, so it won't auto-source your
  `.Renviron`/`.Rprofile`.

# 5. The vscode bridge

The bridge is loopback-only with a per-launch bearer token in a `0600` port
file (see the trust model, §5). Operational hygiene:

- The token rotates on every Positron reload; if you suspect exposure, **reload
  Positron** to mint a fresh one and rewrite the port file.
- `hal_bridge_status()` reports whether it's running and the version.
- The port file lives in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\hal-bridge\port.json` /
  `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/hal-bridge/port.json` — keep that dir owner-only (it is by
  default).

# 6. Running against untrusted inputs

If you must point hal at code/data you don't control (analyzing a third-party
repo, an emailed `.xlsx`, scraped text):

1. Set `permission_policy = "ask"` (or a strict function policy).
2. Set `credential_action = "redact"` or `"block"`.
3. Strip your live credentials from the environment first
   (`Sys.unsetenv("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY")` etc. once the session is auth'd, or run
   in a profile that never had them).
4. Better: run in a throwaway VM/container/dedicated OS user with no access to
   anything sensitive. Guardrails won't contain a prompt-injection payload; OS
   isolation will.

# 7. GitHub / CI hardening (repo side)

For the project repository itself:

- **Enable Dependabot alerts** (free) — surfaces vulnerable transitive deps.
- **Enable secret-scanning push protection** (free) — blocks accidental key
  commits at `git push` time. (hal's history is currently clean.)
- **Protect `main`** — require a PR + passing checks before merge; stops
  unreviewed direct/force-pushes.
- **Pin GitHub Actions to commit SHAs** (not floating `@v2`/`@v4` tags) and
  consider restricting `allowed_actions` to selected/verified — the default
  workflow token is already read-only, which is good.

# 8. One-glance "locked down" profile

```r
hal_configure(
  permission_policy = "ask",
  credential_action = "redact",
  eval_timeout      = 15
)
# plus: untrusted inputs -> throwaway VM/user with no live secrets.
```

Remember the framing from the trust model: these settings reduce blast radius
and stop accidents. For containment against a hostile prompt, isolate at the OS
level.
